intro: Martha Goldstein plays the Third Ballade on an Érard piano built in 1851. Its opening conversation grows into a great A♭-major declaration, with a rocking dance and a storm in C♯ minor along the way.

sections.label: A · Two voices in A♭ major
sections.mNote: Short piano phrases answer one another

sections.label: B · Repeated Cs begin a dance
sections.mNote: Broken octaves introduce a melody with off-beat accents

sections.label: C · Light right-hand runs
sections.mNote: Semiquavers marked leggiero carry the new melody

sections.label: B′ · The dance turns to C♯ minor
sections.mNote: The left hand runs beneath large right-hand chords

sections.label: A′ · The opening returns in octaves
sections.mNote: A♭ major returns with the opening tune enlarged

sections.label: Coda · Runs and four final chords
sections.mNote: The light semiquaver figure returns before the closing chords

cues.title: Two voices answer
cues.text: The piano begins a conversation in A♭ major, marked dolce. Short phrases answer across the keyboard. Their quiet exchange will return near the end, doubled in octaves and filling the piano.
cues.evidence: Opening and final return: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin). Mieczysław Tomaszewski describes the first theme at https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Summer at George Sand’s
cues.text: In the summer of 1841, Chopin writes the Third Ballade under George Sand’s roof at Nohant. The same summer brings the F-minor Fantasy and the two Nocturnes, Op. 48.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski dates the Ballade to summer 1841: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110. The associated works and Nohant setting are summarised from Norbert Müllemann’s Henle preface at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

cues.title: Repeated Cs start dancing
cues.text: The right hand rocks between Cs an octave apart, marked mezza voce — half voice. A new melody grows out of that small gesture. Its accents keep landing between the strong beats.
cues.evidence: Repeated C octaves and mezza voce: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin). Syncopated second theme: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mickiewicz’s water nymph?
cues.text: Schumann wrote in 1841 that Chopin had told him certain poems of Mickiewicz suggested his ballades. For this Third Ballade, tradition names Mickiewicz’s Świtezianka, about a water nymph and a hunter who breaks his oath of faithfulness. Nothing Chopin said ties the poem to this piece.
cues.evidence: Schumann’s 1841 review of the Second Ballade, quoted in Dorota Zakrzewska, ‘Alienation and Powerlessness: Adam Mickiewicz’s Ballady and Chopin’s Ballades’, Polish Music Journal 2 (1999): https://polishmusic.usc.edu/research/publications/polish-music-journal/vol2/mickiewicz-and-chopin/ . The Third Ballade’s usual association with Świtezianka: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

cues.title: Pauline’s name on the score
cues.text: The dedication names Pauline de Noailles, one of Chopin’s pupils. She turns eighteen in the year he writes this Ballade. She dies in 1844, just three years later.
cues.evidence: Dedication: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110. Pauline de Noailles’s dates, 1823–1844, and pupil relationship: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

cues.title: A tune in running notes
cues.text: A third idea arrives in light right-hand semiquavers, marked leggiero. A♭ major is back. The little runs have a tune of their own, which will return once more in the closing bars.
cues.evidence: Leggiero semiquaver theme and its A♭-major reprise: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin). Its brief final return is also described by Tomaszewski.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dance in C♯ minor
cues.text: The rocking idea returns on A♭, then slips into C♯ minor, where that same piano key is written G♯. The left hand races through chromatic runs beneath large right-hand chords.
cues.evidence: The broken-octave theme’s transposition, C♯-minor development and left-hand chromatic runs: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The opening fills the piano
cues.text: A♭ major returns with the opening melody in octaves. The quiet conversation has become a broad declaration, supported by the bass and fuller chords.
cues.evidence: A♭-major return of the opening theme in octaves: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four chords close the door
cues.text: The light A♭-major runs return for a last flourish, followed by a right-hand arpeggio. Four chords end the Ballade. Of Chopin’s four ballades, this is the only one to finish in a major key.
cues.evidence: Closing leggiero runs, arpeggio, four chords and major-key ending: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Repeated Cs set the dance going
transitions.from: A · Two voices in A♭ major
transitions.to: B · Repeated Cs begin a dance
transitions.how: The A♭-major opening settles. The right hand starts rocking between Cs in two octaves, marked mezza voce. Those repeated notes lead into the second theme, whose off-beat accents pull against the steady six-quaver bar.
transitions.evidence: Repeated Cs and mezza voce: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin). Syncopated theme: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110.

transitions.title: The right hand breaks into runs
transitions.from: B · Repeated Cs begin a dance
transitions.how: The rocking theme leads to a new A♭-major idea, carried by right-hand semiquavers marked leggiero. The short, repeated-note gestures open into continuous runs above the left-hand accompaniment.

transitions.title: A♭ becomes G♯
transitions.to: B′ · The dance turns to C♯ minor
transitions.how: The broken-octave figure returns on A♭. A change of key signature turns that note into G♯, the dominant of C♯ minor. The second theme grows into large right-hand chords while the left hand takes up rapid chromatic runs.
transitions.evidence: Transposed broken-octave figure and C♯-minor development: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

transitions.title: A♭ major brings back the opening
transitions.from: B′ · The dance turns to C♯ minor
transitions.to: A′ · The opening returns in octaves
transitions.how: The chromatic left-hand runs widen beyond the octave as the piano builds from piano to forte. The key signature returns to A♭ major, and the opening melody comes back in octaves over the stronger bass.
transitions.evidence: Chromatic retransition, dynamic markings and A♭-major octave return: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

transitions.title: The light runs return
transitions.from: A′ · The opening returns in octaves
transitions.to: Coda · Runs and four final chords
transitions.how: The opening theme’s octave statement leads to the A♭-major leggiero runs. The right hand recalls the third idea, sweeps through an arpeggio, and joins the left hand for four closing chords.
transitions.evidence: Final return of the third theme and four-chord close: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/110 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._3_(Chopin).

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
